experiments.title: Kafka Consumer Offset Commit Race
experiments.subtitle: Rebalance mid-batch causes uncommitted offsets to replay as duplicate payments
experiments.scenario:
A payment processing service consumes from a Kafka topic with manual offset commit (`enable.auto.commit=false`). The consumer polls a batch of 50 payment events, processes each one by inserting into PostgreSQL, then calls `commitSync()` once at the end of the batch. When the service is slow under load, the Kafka broker triggers a group rebalance before the batch finishes. The partition is reassigned to another consumer instance, which re-reads all uncommitted offsets and processes those payments again.

This scenario is especially dangerous in fintech because the duplicate processing window is proportional to batch size: a batch of 50 payments can all be duplicated, not just one. The root cause is the gap between record processing completion and offset commit, combined with a rebalance that closes that window without committing.
experiments.impact: Duplicate payments charged to customer cards or debited from accounts. Each rebalance event during high load can duplicate an entire batch. With batch sizes of 50-100 and rebalances triggered every few minutes under load, hundreds of duplicate transactions can accumulate before monitoring catches the anomaly.

experiments.failureExplanation: Kafka's consumer group protocol allows the broker to trigger a rebalance if a consumer exceeds `max.poll.interval.ms` without polling again. When slow DB inserts delay the loop, the consumer misses its poll deadline, the partition is revoked and reassigned to another instance, and that new instance starts reading from the last committed offset. Because `commitSync()` was never reached, every record processed in the current batch is replayed. Without idempotency guards, each replayed record produces a duplicate payment insert.

assessment.text: A Kafka consumer processes records and calls commitSync() at the end of each batch. A rebalance occurs mid-batch. What is the most likely outcome?
options: A) The in-flight batch is rolled back and no records are processed
B) The partition is reassigned and another consumer re-processes uncommitted records from the last committed offset
C) Kafka's exactly-once guarantee prevents any re-processing automatically
D) The original consumer retains the partition until it finishes the batch
assessment.explanation: Kafka reassigns the partition to another consumer starting from the last committed offset. Because the in-flight batch was not committed, those records are replayed. Kafka does NOT provide exactly-once by default — that requires explicit EOS configuration.

assessment.text: Which two mechanisms together provide the strongest guarantee against duplicate payment inserts after a Kafka rebalance?
options: A) Increasing batch size and decreasing poll interval
B) commitSync() per record + idempotent DB upsert (UNIQUE constraint + ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING)
C) enable.auto.commit=true with a short auto-commit interval
D) Storing offsets in the application database instead of Kafka
assessment.explanation: Per-record commitSync() minimises the uncommitted window so fewer records are replayed. The idempotent upsert ensures that any record that IS replayed does not produce a duplicate row. Auto-commit (C) is unreliable under rebalance. Storing offsets in the DB (D) is a valid advanced pattern but is significantly more complex to implement correctly.

assessment.text: What is the purpose of ConsumerRebalanceListener.onPartitionsRevoked() in the context of offset management?
options: A) To pause the consumer and wait for all in-flight messages to be acknowledged by producers
B) To commit offsets for currently-assigned partitions before they are handed off to another consumer
C) To reset consumer group offsets to the earliest position after a failure
D) To register new partition assignments with the group coordinator
assessment.explanation: onPartitionsRevoked() is called just before the consumer loses ownership of its partitions. Committing in-flight offsets here ensures the new partition owner starts from the correct position, not from the last periodic commit — which may be stale by seconds or more.

experiments.title: Zombie Consumer After Group Rebalance
experiments.subtitle: Network-partitioned consumer continues processing — same records handled by two instances simultaneously
experiments.scenario:
A Kafka consumer group member (Consumer-1) experiences a network partition: its TCP connection to the broker is interrupted but the process itself keeps running. The group coordinator waits for `session.timeout.ms` (default: 45 seconds) before declaring the member dead. During that 45-second window, Consumer-1 continues reading from its local buffer and processing payment records. After the timeout, the coordinator reassigns the partition to Consumer-2, which also starts processing from the last committed offset. Both consumers are now processing overlapping record ranges simultaneously.

This 'zombie consumer' window is proportional to `session.timeout.ms`. With the default of 45 seconds and a throughput of 500 events/second, up to 22,500 payment records may be processed twice before the partition is cleanly handed off.
experiments.impact: Every payment processed during the zombie window is a candidate for duplication. At 500 events/second with a 45-second zombie window, up to 22,500 duplicate payment attempts can occur in a single incident. Chargebacks from customers who were double-billed can cost 3-5x the original transaction value in fees and penalties.
incorrectCode: // application.properties — dangerously loose Kafka consumer settings
# session.timeout.ms default is 45000 — zombie window is 45 seconds!
# No group.instance.id set — dynamic membership, full rebalance on every join/leave
// No idempotency check — assumes Kafka delivers each event once

experiments.failureExplanation: When a network partition isolates Consumer-1 from the Kafka broker, the coordinator cannot receive heartbeats. After `session.timeout.ms` elapses, the partition is reassigned and Consumer-2 begins processing. However, Consumer-1's process is still alive and has buffered records from its last successful `poll()`. It continues calling `processPayment()` on those records until the network recovers (and it discovers it has lost partition ownership on the next metadata refresh). During this overlap period both consumers process the same records, and without idempotency guards both inserts succeed.

Static membership (`group.instance.id`) eliminates unnecessary full rebalances during rolling restarts. Idempotent upsert in `insertIfAbsent()` ensures that any records processed by both the zombie and the replacement consumer are deduplicated at the database layer.

assessment.text: What is a 'zombie consumer' in the context of Kafka consumer groups?
options: A) A consumer that has committed offsets but stopped processing new records
B) A consumer whose process is still running and processing records after the coordinator has declared it dead and reassigned its partitions
C) A consumer that is intentionally paused for maintenance during a rolling deployment
D) A consumer that reads from a compacted topic and receives only the latest value per key
assessment.explanation: A zombie consumer is a live process that continues processing records after the group coordinator has timed it out and reassigned its partitions to another consumer. The zombie is unaware of the reassignment until its next metadata refresh, creating a window where two consumers process the same records simultaneously.

assessment.text: Reducing session.timeout.ms from 45s to 6s has which primary trade-off?
options: A) Increased network bandwidth consumption from more frequent partition metadata fetches
B) Higher risk of false rebalances triggered by GC pauses or brief network hiccups exceeding the timeout
C) Reduced consumer throughput because heartbeats compete with poll() on the same thread
D) Incompatibility with static membership (group.instance.id)
assessment.explanation: With a 6s session timeout, any GC pause, pod CPU throttle, or transient network delay exceeding the heartbeat interval can cause the coordinator to declare the consumer dead and trigger a rebalance. This is mitigated by tuning JVM GC pause targets below the heartbeat interval and using static membership to reduce rebalance frequency.

assessment.text: Why does static membership (group.instance.id) reduce the zombie consumer risk during rolling deployments?
options: A) It prevents the coordinator from ever timing out consumer members, eliminating zombie scenarios entirely
B) It allows a restarted consumer to rejoin the group and reclaim its previous partitions without triggering a full rebalance, reducing the window where partitions are unassigned
C) It synchronises offsets between consumer instances using a shared in-memory cache
D) It disables session timeouts for the named instance so deployments can proceed without rebalance overhead
assessment.explanation: With static membership, when a consumer with a known group.instance.id restarts and rejoins, the coordinator reassigns its previous partitions directly without a full stop-the-world rebalance. This means the partition unassigned window is minimal (just the restart time), reducing both rebalance overhead and the probability of a zombie scenario during routine deployments.

experiments.title: Redis Cache Stampede on Balance Read
experiments.subtitle: Simultaneous TTL expiry floods PostgreSQL with 1000 concurrent identical queries
experiments.scenario:
A high-volume merchant's account balance is cached in Redis with a fixed 60-second TTL. At exactly 09:00:00.000, the TTL expires. In the next 50 milliseconds, 1,000 concurrent API requests (balance checks for real-time payment decisions) all miss the cache simultaneously. All 1,000 threads proceed to query PostgreSQL for the same account balance. The database connection pool saturates, query latency spikes to 8 seconds, and some requests return stale data from before the TTL expired because different threads store slightly different values depending on query timing.

This pattern — the 'thundering herd' or 'cache stampede' — is especially damaging in fintech because balance reads directly gate payment authorisation decisions. When the DB is overwhelmed by stampede traffic, legitimate payment requests are rejected with timeout errors, causing revenue loss and customer frustration.
experiments.impact: A single stampede event can saturate the PostgreSQL connection pool for 5-10 seconds, rejecting all payment authorisation requests during that window. For a merchant processing $10,000/minute, a 10-second outage costs $1,667 in lost transactions. Hot accounts (large merchants) can stampede on every 60-second cache cycle if traffic exceeds the stampede threshold.
incorrectCode: // UNSAFE: 1000 concurrent threads all reach here simultaneously on TTL expiry

incorrectAnnotations.note: UNSAFE: no lock or coordination — all cache-miss threads race to query the DB
RACE: 1000 concurrent DB queries for the same accountId when TTL expires

experiments.failureExplanation: When the Redis TTL expires, all concurrent requests find `cached == null` before any of them has had a chance to repopulate the cache. The check-then-fetch-then-set sequence is not atomic, so N threads each independently fetch from PostgreSQL and independently set the cache. The database sees N identical queries simultaneously. With a hot merchant account and high traffic, N can exceed the connection pool size, causing pool exhaustion and cascading failures across all payment authorisation endpoints.

correctCode: // Single-flight: only one thread fetches from DB; others wait then read cache
// Double-check after acquiring lock — previous holder may have populated cache
// Jitter: randomise TTL ±10s to stagger future stampedes
experiments.correctExplanation: The single-flight pattern uses a Redisson distributed lock so that only one thread queries PostgreSQL on cache miss; all other threads block on the lock and then read the freshly populated value (double-checked after acquiring). TTL jitter (±10 seconds) staggers expiry across multiple hot accounts, preventing coordinated stampedes from hitting at the same wall-clock second.

alternatives.name: Probabilistic Early Expiration (XFetch Algorithm)
code: // XFetch: proactively recompute cache before TTL expires
// No lock needed — only the thread that 'wins the lottery' recomputes
pros: No distributed lock — zero lock contention
Naturally distributes recomputation across request threads before expiry
cons: Multiple threads may recompute simultaneously if traffic is very high
Requires storing compute delta time alongside cached value
alternatives.whenToUse: For read-heavy caches with steady traffic where lock contention would itself become a bottleneck. Combine with TTL jitter for best results.

experiments.performanceNotes: The distributed lock adds ~1-2ms latency for cache-miss requests (Redis round-trip for lock acquisition). Under normal operation (cache hit rate >99%), this overhead is irrelevant. The key benefit is that DB query rate under stampede conditions drops from O(N concurrent requests) to O(1). TTL jitter adds negligible overhead but prevents coordinated multi-account stampedes.

+1-2ms latency on cache miss; best safety

Simple to add; doesn't eliminate stampede for single key

assessment.text: What condition triggers a cache stampede, and why is it particularly severe for a single hot key?
options: A) A cache stampede occurs when the Redis server runs out of memory and evicts multiple keys simultaneously
B) A cache stampede occurs when a cached key's TTL expires and many concurrent requests all miss the cache before any thread repopulates it, causing all of them to query the database simultaneously
C) A cache stampede occurs when write-heavy traffic invalidates the cache faster than reads can populate it
D) A cache stampede occurs when multiple Redis replicas have inconsistent values for the same key
assessment.explanation: A cache stampede (thundering herd) is triggered when a TTL expiry creates a window where many concurrent requests all observe a cache miss before any single thread has had time to fetch and store the new value. For a hot key (high QPS), this window admits a large number of simultaneous DB queries. The DB is then hit N times for the same data where N is the concurrent request rate during the expiry window.

assessment.text: Why is it essential to perform a double-check (re-read the cache) after acquiring the distributed lock in the single-flight pattern?
options: A) Because Redis may have evicted the key between the lock acquisition and the double-check
B) Because the thread that was waiting for the lock may have been the first to acquire it, so the cache might still be empty
C) Because the thread that acquired the lock before you may have already populated the cache while you were waiting — skipping the DB query avoids a redundant fetch
D) Because Redisson locks do not guarantee mutual exclusion and the cache may have been written by multiple threads simultaneously
assessment.explanation: While a thread waits for the lock, the previous lock holder may have already fetched the balance and populated the cache. Without the double-check, the newly unblocked thread would proceed to query the DB unnecessarily. The double-check ensures that only the first thread through the lock makes a DB call; all subsequent threads read from the already-populated cache.

assessment.text: How does TTL jitter help prevent cache stampedes across multiple accounts?
options: A) It increases the cache TTL so that keys expire less frequently, reducing the total number of stampede events
B) It randomises each key's expiry time so that many keys do not expire at the exact same wall-clock second, spreading DB load over time
C) It makes the TTL proportional to account balance so that high-value accounts are cached longer
D) It signals to Redis to use probabilistic eviction instead of exact TTL expiry
assessment.explanation: Without jitter, all accounts cached at the same time (e.g., during application startup or a mass cache warm) will expire simultaneously, causing a coordinated stampede across all keys at once. TTL jitter (e.g., base_ttl ± random_seconds) staggers expiry times so that keys expire at different times, distributing cache-miss DB queries evenly over the jitter window rather than concentrating them in a single spike.

experiments.title: Distributed Lock Expiry During Financial Operation
experiments.subtitle: Redis lock TTL shorter than payment processing time allows duplicate transaction execution
experiments.scenario:
A payment deduplication service uses a Redisson distributed lock to ensure each payment reference is processed exactly once across multiple service instances. The lock is acquired with a fixed TTL of 5 seconds (`lock.lock(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS)`). Under normal load this is sufficient. However, when the downstream card processor is slow (a cold start, network congestion, or external API latency spike), payment processing takes 6-8 seconds. The lock expires at the 5-second mark while the first service instance is still processing. A second instance sees no lock, acquires it, and begins processing the same payment. Both instances complete successfully — the customer is charged twice.

This failure mode is insidious because it only manifests under degraded conditions: exactly when the system is already under stress from slow external dependencies. Normal load testing will never surface it.
experiments.impact: Each occurrence results in a double-charge to the customer's card. The second charge is usually identical in amount and merchant, making it immediately visible to customers. Card processor chargeback rate spikes, triggering fraud alerts. At scale, even a 0.01% duplicate rate across millions of transactions represents thousands of double-charges per day.
incorrectCode: // UNSAFE: fixed TTL of 5s — expires if card processor takes >5s
throw new DuplicatePaymentException("Payment already in progress");
// Card processor may take 6-8s under load — lock expires mid-operation!
// If lock expired, unlock() is a no-op — another thread already acquired it

incorrectAnnotations.note: UNSAFE: 5-second TTL is shorter than the card processor p99 latency under load (6-8s)
RACE: lock expires here — second instance acquires lock and starts processing same payment
UNSAFE: isHeldByCurrentThread() returns false after expiry — unlock() is skipped, but duplicate already running

experiments.failureExplanation: When the lock TTL (5s) is shorter than the operation duration (6-8s), the lock expires while the first thread is mid-execution. Redisson does not automatically extend a lock created with an explicit TTL — extension only happens for locks created without a TTL (the watchdog pattern). Once the lock expires, any other instance can acquire it and begin the same operation. Both instances complete the card charge successfully because neither detects the other's in-progress state.

correctCode: // lock() without TTL: Redisson watchdog auto-extends every leaseTime/3
lock.lock();  // default leaseTime=30s, watchdog renews every 10s
// Double-check: return existing result if already processed
// Idempotent save: UNIQUE constraint on reference prevents dual-write
experiments.correctExplanation: Using `lock.lock()` without a TTL enables Redisson's watchdog mechanism, which automatically extends the lock's lease every 10 seconds (leaseTime/3) as long as the owning thread is alive. The lock only expires if the JVM process dies, preventing mid-operation expiry. The double-check inside the lock plus idempotent DB save (UNIQUE constraint on `reference`) provide defense-in-depth against any residual race.

alternatives.name: Conservative Fixed TTL (3x expected duration)
code: // If watchdog is not acceptable (e.g., process crash must release lock quickly),
// set TTL to 3x the p99 processing time with idempotency as safety net
// Always pair with idempotent DB write as defense-in-depth
pros: Lock will eventually auto-release after process crash (no manual cleanup needed)

assessment.text: What is the Redisson watchdog mechanism and when does it activate?
options: A) A background process that monitors Redis memory usage and evicts expired locks when memory is low
B) An automatic lock lease renewal mechanism that activates when a lock is acquired without an explicit TTL, extending the lock every leaseTime/3 seconds while the owning thread is alive
C) A circuit breaker that prevents new lock acquisitions when Redis latency exceeds a threshold
D) A periodic task that checks for orphaned locks left by crashed processes and removes them after a grace period
assessment.explanation: The Redisson watchdog is a background timer that automatically calls PEXPIRE on the lock key every leaseTime/3 seconds (default: every 10s for a 30s leaseTime). It ONLY activates when the lock is acquired via lock() without an explicit TTL argument. If the JVM process dies, the watchdog stops and the lock expires after the remaining leaseTime — ensuring automatic cleanup of locks from crashed processes.

assessment.text: Why should a distributed lock NOT be the sole protection against duplicate payment processing?
options: A) Because distributed locks have too much latency for high-frequency payment workloads
B) Because Redis can fail or the lock can expire (e.g., network partition, GC pause, process crash), and the DB-level idempotency constraint provides protection even when the lock fails
C) Because lock contention serialises all payment requests, reducing throughput to single-threaded levels
D) Because Redisson does not support lock acquisition retries in a cluster configuration
assessment.explanation: Distributed locks are a coordination mechanism, not a data integrity guarantee. Redis failures, network partitions, process crashes, and even clock skew can cause locks to behave unexpectedly. A UNIQUE constraint on the payment reference at the database layer ensures that even if two instances somehow both run the charge operation, only one can commit successfully. Defense-in-depth requires both the lock (for coordination) and the DB constraint (for correctness).

assessment.text: What is the correct Redisson API call to prevent lock expiry during a variable-duration financial operation?
options: A) lock.tryLock(30, 300, TimeUnit.SECONDS) — wait up to 30s, hold for 300s
B) lock.lock() — no TTL argument, enables watchdog auto-renewal
C) lock.lock(60, TimeUnit.SECONDS) — explicit 60s TTL as a safety margin
D) lock.lockInterruptibly() — allows the lock to be interrupted and re-acquired
assessment.explanation: lock.lock() without a leaseTime argument is the correct form. It sets an internal lease (default 30s) and starts the watchdog timer, which renews the lease every 10s automatically. Any form that specifies an explicit TTL (options A and C) disables the watchdog — the lock WILL expire at the specified time regardless of whether the operation is complete.

experiments.title: CDC Reconciliation Gap (Out-of-Order Event Capture)
experiments.subtitle: Debezium connector restart causes duplicate CDC events, corrupting reconciliation totals
experiments.scenario:
A financial reconciliation system uses Debezium to capture changes from PostgreSQL's WAL (Write-Ahead Log) and stream them to Kafka for downstream processing. During a 30-second network blip, the Debezium connector loses its Kafka Connect worker connection and restarts. On restart, it resumes from its last committed Kafka offset — but due to the restart, some WAL events between the last offset and the restart point are re-read and published to Kafka a second time. The reconciliation consumer naively appends all received events to its `reconciliation_events` table without checking for duplicates. The end-of-day reconciliation job then counts credit/debit pairs and produces an incorrect daily settlement total.

This failure is particularly dangerous because it is silent: no exception is thrown, no alert fires, and the reconciliation totals look plausible. The error is typically discovered during end-of-day settlement when the total does not match the card processor's report.
experiments.impact: Duplicate CDC events inflate reconciliation totals by the number of re-processed transactions. In a system processing $50M/day with 10,000 transactions, a Debezium restart that duplicates 200 transactions can overstate the settlement total by $200,000-$2M depending on transaction sizes. This discrepancy triggers a manual reconciliation process costing 4-8 hours of analyst time per incident.

experiments.failureExplanation: Debezium uses Kafka offsets to track its position in the PostgreSQL WAL. When the connector restarts, it reads its last committed Kafka offset and resumes publication from that point. Any WAL changes that were published to Kafka but whose Kafka offsets were not committed before the restart will be re-published. The reconciliation consumer receives these events a second time and, without deduplication logic, inserts them again. The resulting duplicate rows inflate aggregate totals in the reconciliation query.

assessment.text: Why does Debezium sometimes re-deliver CDC events after a connector restart?
options: A) Because PostgreSQL WAL entries are inherently unreliable and can be re-emitted by the database

B) Because Debezium uses at-least-once delivery semantics: it resumes from its last committed Kafka offset on restart, and any events published after that offset but before the restart are re-published
C) Because Kafka automatically replays all messages in a topic when a new consumer group is created
D) Because Debezium buffers events in memory and flushes them on restart to prevent data loss
assessment.explanation: Debezium is an at-least-once system by default. It periodically commits its WAL read position as a Kafka offset. If the connector restarts before committing its latest position, it resumes from the last committed position and re-reads WAL events that were already published. This is by design — it prevents data loss at the cost of potential duplicates, which the consumer is expected to handle with idempotent logic.

assessment.text: Why is INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING preferred over SELECT COUNT(*) > 0 ... INSERT for CDC deduplication?
options: A) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING has lower CPU overhead because it uses a hash index instead of a B-tree index
B) SELECT-then-INSERT is a check-then-act pattern with a TOCTOU race: two concurrent duplicate events can both see count=0 and both insert. ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING is atomic at the database level
C) ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING automatically retries the insert if the conflict is temporary
D) SELECT COUNT(*) requires a full table scan and is too slow for high-volume CDC processing
assessment.explanation: SELECT COUNT(*) > 0 ... INSERT is a classic check-then-act race condition: under concurrent delivery, two threads can both observe count=0 before either inserts, then both insert successfully — producing a duplicate. INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING is a single atomic SQL operation: the duplicate check and the insert happen in the same statement with the database's MVCC isolation guaranteeing correctness under concurrency.

assessment.text: A reconciliation job runs: SELECT SUM(amount) FROM reconciliation_events WHERE type = 'CREDIT'. After a Debezium restart, this returns $502,000 instead of the expected $500,000. What is the most likely root cause?
options: A) PostgreSQL MVCC read isolation is showing uncommitted transactions in the sum
B) The Debezium connector re-delivered $2,000 of CREDIT events from before the restart, which were inserted again due to missing idempotency logic
C) Kafka consumer offset management committed offsets from a future batch, skipping some events
D) The reconciliation query is missing a WHERE clause to filter by processing date
assessment.explanation: A $2,000 overstatement after a Debezium restart is the textbook symptom of duplicate CDC event insertion. The restart caused re-delivery of previously processed CREDIT events, which were inserted again because the consumer lacked ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING protection. The overstatement amount equals the sum of re-delivered CREDIT transaction amounts.

experiments.title: Rate Limiter Race Under Concurrent Pressure
experiments.subtitle: Redis INCR + EXPIRE non-atomicity allows 10% more requests to slip through than the configured limit
experiments.scenario:
An API gateway enforces a rate limit of 100 requests per minute per merchant using a Redis counter (`INCR rl:{merchantId}` + `EXPIRE rl:{merchantId} 60`). Under normal load this works. During a Black Friday burst, 110 concurrent requests arrive within 1 millisecond. All 110 threads call INCR simultaneously — none has yet called EXPIRE. All 110 INCRs succeed because the key does not yet exist and each INCR atomically creates it and increments it. All 110 threads then call `if count == 1 then EXPIRE`. Only the thread that incremented to 1 sets the TTL. The other 109 threads proceed to check `if count > 100` — 10 of them see count > 100 but are past the check by the time the EXPIRE fires.

The net result: 110 requests pass through instead of 100, and the rate limiter key now exists with the correct TTL — so for the remaining 59 seconds, the limit works correctly. But for every burst at a new minute boundary, up to 110 requests will slip through instead of 100.
experiments.impact: A 10% rate limit bypass may seem minor, but in fintech rate limits often protect downstream payment processors that charge per-transaction or enforce strict contractual API quotas. Exceeding a card processor's API rate limit triggers HTTP 429 errors, failed payments, and potential account suspension. For a merchant processing $1M/hour, 10% excess requests during burst windows can generate $100K in failed transactions per hour of overload.

// RACE: 110 threads all do INCR before any does EXPIRE
// Only the thread that gets count==1 sets TTL
// But all 110 threads already hold their count values and proceed

incorrectAnnotations.note: UNSAFE: INCR and EXPIRE are non-atomic — concurrent threads all INCR before any EXPIRE fires
RACE: 110 threads all reach count==1 through 110 before this if-block completes for the first thread
UNSAFE: by the time count > MAX_REQUESTS is evaluated, the INCR already happened — the counter is permanently inflated

experiments.failureExplanation: Redis INCR is atomic per-command, but the INCR + EXPIRE sequence is not. When 110 threads all send INCR simultaneously, Redis processes them sequentially (single-threaded command execution) and returns values 1 through 110. Each thread then independently evaluates `count == 1` — only the thread that received count=1 calls EXPIRE. The remaining 109 threads skip EXPIRE and check `count > 100`. Threads with count 101-110 should be rejected, but threads 1-100 (and thread with count=1 which also sets EXPIRE) all pass through. If the EXPIRE had not been set yet when threads 1-110 finished their checks, the key would remain without a TTL — causing the counter to persist indefinitely and block all subsequent requests until a Redis restart.

Redis's single-threaded Lua execution guarantees that no other command can interleave between the INCR and EXPIRE within the script. This eliminates the race window completely — either the TTL is set in the same atomic operation as the first INCR, or it was already set by a previous script execution.

assessment.text: Why does the INCR + EXPIRE rate limiter allow more than MAX_REQUESTS requests under concurrent burst conditions?
options: A) Because Redis INCR is not thread-safe and can return the same value to multiple concurrent callers

B) Because INCR and EXPIRE are two separate non-atomic commands: all concurrent threads call INCR before any calls EXPIRE, so the TTL window may start late or not at all, and all threads have already received their count values before the rejection check
C) Because Redis single-threaded execution serialises INCRs, causing thread starvation under burst load
D) Because the EXPIRE command resets the counter to zero, inadvertently allowing a new window to start mid-burst
assessment.explanation: Redis INCR is atomic per-command — it correctly returns sequential values to concurrent callers. The problem is that INCR and EXPIRE are two separate round-trips with no atomicity between them. Under burst load, 110 threads can all complete their INCRs before any thread issues its EXPIRE. All 110 threads then proceed to their count > MAX_REQUESTS check. Without the TTL being set atomically, there is also risk of the key persisting forever if the process crashes between INCR and EXPIRE.

assessment.text: Why does a Redis Lua script solve the INCR + EXPIRE race condition?
options: A) Because Lua scripts execute faster than individual Redis commands, reducing the time window for race conditions
B) Because Redis executes Lua scripts atomically — no other command can be processed between the INCR and EXPIRE within the script, eliminating the race window entirely
C) Because Lua scripts automatically retry on failure, ensuring the EXPIRE command always eventually executes
D) Because Redis Lua scripts use optimistic locking (WATCH/MULTI/EXEC) to detect concurrent modifications
assessment.explanation: Redis is single-threaded for command execution, and Lua scripts are executed as a single atomic unit. No other Redis command from any other client can be processed between the INCR and EXPIRE inside a Lua script. This guarantees that the TTL is always set in the same atomic step as the first INCR — the race window between the two commands is completely eliminated.

assessment.text: A rate limiter with MAX_REQUESTS=100 and WINDOW_SECONDS=60 uses the buggy INCR+EXPIRE pattern. Redis TTL rl:merchant-99 returns -1 (no expiry). What is the most likely consequence?
options: A) The rate limiter will correctly reset at the next minute boundary because INCR automatically resets when the key reaches MAX_REQUESTS
B) The counter will persist indefinitely without resetting, permanently blocking the merchant until an operator manually deletes the key or Redis restarts
C) Redis will automatically garbage-collect the key after 60 seconds because it recognises the INCR pattern
D) The rate limiter will switch to a fallback mode and allow all requests until the key is recreated
assessment.explanation: A Redis key with TTL=-1 has no expiry set and will persist indefinitely. If the counter reached 110 (above the limit) during the burst and no EXPIRE was ever set (the race condition), every subsequent request will see count=110 (or higher as INCR continues) and be rejected forever. The merchant is effectively permanently blocked until an operator manually runs DEL rl:merchant-99. This is a silent availability incident — no exception is thrown, requests just appear to be rate-limited.
